intro.title: Not a news digest — a shared space for ideas
intro.text: This magazine is not a record of events. It is an attempt to bring ideas, lived experience, research, public sentiment and new possibilities onto one page. We want researchers, teachers, journalists, activists, policymakers, students, writers and ordinary citizens to have an equal say here.
intro.quote: The future of any region is shaped less by plans and announcements than by an aware society, engaged citizens and honest conversation.

items.title: Society
items.short: Migration, livelihoods, village life, social change and public concerns.
description: Hill society is changing fast. Villages are emptying out, the search for work is pulling young people to the plains, and old social structures are taking new shapes.
Under this theme we look at migration, livelihoods, village life, social change and public concerns — through both lived experience on the ground and research.

items.title: Culture
items.short: Folk traditions, folk literature, music, language, history and heritage.
description: The Himalaya's identity lives in its folk traditions, dialects, songs and festivals. This heritage has been handed down for generations, and today it is also at risk of fading.
Here we try to understand and keep alive folk traditions, folk literature, music, language, history and cultural heritage.

items.title: Environment
items.short: Climate change, glaciers, forests, biodiversity and natural resources.
description: The Himalaya is not just mountains — it holds the water sources and biodiversity that hundreds of millions depend on. Climate change and growing pressure on resources are straining that balance.
This theme brings a fact-based, balanced look at climate change, glaciers, forests, biodiversity and natural resources.

items.title: Education
items.short: School and higher education, research, innovation and the challenges young people face.
description: Access to good schooling in remote hill areas is still a big question. At the same time, young people here are finding new paths in research, technology and innovation.
We bring out the experience of teachers, students and experts on school education, higher education, research, innovation and the challenges facing the young.

items.title: Health
items.short: Healthcare in the hills, public health, maternal and child health, and AYUSH.
description: Mountain geography shapes who can reach a doctor and how fast. Distance, roads and resources make health a very different question in the hills.
This theme gives space to experience and ideas on mountain health systems, public health, maternal and child health, and AYUSH.

items.title: Development
items.short: Tourism, agriculture, enterprise, infrastructure, policy and governance.
description: What kind of development suits the mountains? The question is old, and it has never mattered more. Finding the balance between development and conservation is the key to the Himalaya's future.
Here we try to open a real conversation between policymakers and society on tourism, farming, enterprise, infrastructure, policy and governance.

items.title: Changing Weather, Melting Glaciers: Climate Change Arrives in the Himalaya
items.excerpt: How shifting patterns of snow, rain and glacier melt are showing up in the hills' water sources, farms and daily life.
summary: The article opens with a simple question: is climate change a distant scientific debate for people in the hills, or an everyday reality? It looks at how changing weather is affecting fields, springs and seasonal livelihoods.
Putting local experience next to available studies, it asks how villages, panchayats and policymakers can each prepare to adapt.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Emptying Villages: Why People Leave, and What Might Bring Them Back
items.excerpt: Scarce jobs, schools and services are hollowing out hill villages. Is there a realistic way home?
summary: Out-migration is the most talked-about and most stubborn challenge facing the Himalayan states. This piece tries to understand what pushes families to leave their villages.
It also looks at the small efforts of those who have returned and are starting again with farming, tourism or small enterprises.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Folk Traditions and a New Generation: Keeping a Heritage Alive
items.excerpt: Folk songs, festivals and dialects hold a people's memory. How does that heritage survive changing lifestyles?
summary: Folk traditions are not just entertainment — they are a community's shared memory. The article asks where folk songs, instruments and dialects stand as towns grow and lifestyles change.
It also points to young people who are carrying this heritage forward through new mediums.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Water, Forest and Land: Communities and Their Commons
items.excerpt: Where the hills' tradition of community rights over natural resources — and community care for them — stands today.
summary: In hill villages, water, forests and land were long managed as a shared responsibility. This piece sets out the strengths of that tradition and the pressures it now faces.
It also asks how local communities can be given a stronger role in conservation at the level of policy.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Schools in the Hills: A Question of Access, Quality and Trust
items.excerpt: What conditions schools in remote villages are working in, and what could make them better.
summary: Falling enrolment, too few teachers and long walks to class — many hill schools face all three. The article looks at these conditions through the eyes of teachers and parents.
It also discusses experiments that are creating better places to learn with very limited means.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Healthcare for Remote Villages: Hard Problems, Real Possibilities
items.excerpt: Bad roads, long distances and thin resources — how can healthcare in the hills be made reachable?
summary: In the hills, falling ill often begins with a long journey. This piece lays out the basic challenges of mountain healthcare, with a close look at maternal and child health.
It also considers the role of local health workers and what technology could realistically offer.
items.author: Author name

items.title: The Rural Economy of the Hills: Farming, Livestock and New Openings
items.excerpt: From traditional farming to homestays and local produce — ways to put the village economy on firmer ground.
summary: For a long time the hill economy rested on farming and livestock. The article asks how solid that foundation still is.
It also discusses new openings in local produce, rural tourism and small enterprise.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Women of the Hills: Labour, Leadership and Empowerment
items.excerpt: Women have always carried the hill economy — in the fields, the forest and the home. Today they are leading too.
summary: Much of life in the hills rests on women's work. This piece is an attempt to recognise that contribution and understand the challenges women face.
It also draws attention to the growing leadership of women in self-help groups, panchayats and local initiatives.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Young People of the Himalaya: Aspirations, Opportunities and Their Role
items.excerpt: What does a generation shaping itself between education, technology and enterprise actually want?
summary: A new generation in the Himalayan regions is building its identity between education, jobs, technology, enterprise and global opportunity. This article sets out their hopes and their hurdles.
It also asks how young people can become participants in change rather than spectators.
items.author: Author name

items.title: Developing the Himalaya: In Search of Balance
items.excerpt: Roads, dams and tourism are real needs. How do we meet them without breaking a fragile mountain ecology?
summary: The hills need development — but at what cost? This piece raises the question of environmental balance alongside infrastructure, tourism and energy projects.
Its argument is that development policy for the Himalaya has to be built with local communities and a real understanding of the environment.

items.label: First Issue
items.title: Why the Himalaya Needs a Conversation
items.description: A magazine's first issue is more than the start of publication. It introduces the ideas, purpose and direction the magazine means to follow. This first issue of Himalaya Samvad comes to you in that spirit.

editorial.title: Why the Himalaya Needs a Conversation
paragraphs: A magazine's first issue is more than a formal start to publishing. It introduces the ideas, the purpose and the direction the magazine means to follow. This first issue of Himalaya Samvad comes to you in that spirit. It marks the beginning of a forum whose aim is to carry forward a serious, meaningful and wide-ranging conversation about the Himalaya and the people who live there.

The Himalaya is not just a chain of mountains. It underpins the culture, traditions, way of life, livelihoods and faith of hundreds of millions of people. Many of the country's great rivers begin here, and its ecology shapes a vast stretch of land far beyond the hills. And yet so many Himalayan questions — ecological balance, climate change, migration, education, health, jobs, the protection of culture, the challenges of development — rarely get the serious attention they deserve.

The Himalaya is passing through a time when the need to find a balance — between development and conservation, tradition and modernity, local needs and global pressures — is felt more sharply than ever. At such a time, conversation is not a choice; it is a necessity. That is why we chose the theme of our first issue: “Why the Himalaya needs a conversation.”

The theme is not just a question. It is an invitation to think together. We believe that understanding the issues that will decide the Himalaya's future, and finding answers to them, means bringing different viewpoints, experiences and ideas into the same room. Dialogue is what can build a bridge between society, policy, research and public feeling.

This issue carries articles on education, health, the environment, culture, water, forests and land, migration, the rural economy, women's empowerment, the role of young people, and Himalayan development. Through them we have tried to look at the Himalaya from many sides, and to help our readers do the same.

Our aim is not only to inform, but to provoke thought, bring hard questions into the open and strengthen a culture of constructive debate. We hope this issue will give readers, researchers, teachers, policymakers, social workers and engaged citizens something real to talk about.
editorial.pullQuote: At such a time, conversation is not a choice; it is a necessity.

intro.title: Committed to the questions that matter in the hills
paragraphs: The editorial board of Himalaya Samvad brings together people with very different backgrounds, views and areas of expertise. What they share is a commitment to understanding the questions facing Himalayan society seriously, sensitively and on the basis of facts — and to bringing them to our readers. The board draws on long experience in journalism, education, literature, the environment, social science, culture, health, administration and public life.

We believe any real conversation rests on respect for different viewpoints and an open exchange of ideas. The board's job is not only to choose and edit what we publish, but to make sure the magazine presents the real concerns, challenges, achievements and possibilities of Himalayan society in a way that is balanced and can be trusted.

members.name: Mukesh Prasad Bahuguna
members.bio: A former Air Force serviceman, teacher, independent commentator and satirist, Mukesh Prasad Bahuguna has served as state vice-president of the Uttarakhand Government Teachers' Association. Widely known as ‘Mirchi Baba’, his articles and satire have appeared in many newspapers and magazines. His writing is sharp and to the point on the social issues and public concerns of the day.

members.name: Vinay K.D.
members.bio: A senior IT professional, independent journalist and writer, Vinay K.D. is the founder and editor-in-chief of Himalaya Samvad. For fifteen years he has been writing and holding public conversations on Himalayan society, the environment, culture, rural tourism, village life and development. He is known for speaking up on Himalayan concerns, the voices of local communities and sustainable development.

members.name: Vijaypal Rawat
members.bio: Executive Editor of Himalaya Samvad, Vijaypal Rawat is a social activist from Uttarakhand and a familiar name in public causes. He has long been active on water, forests and land, migration, environmental protection and disaster relief. His clear and outspoken stand on public-interest issues has earned him a distinct place across the hill regions.

members.name: Akhilesh Dimri
members.bio: A senior development professional, social thinker and rural development specialist, Akhilesh Dimri has spent two decades working on livelihoods, community empowerment, natural resource management and corporate social responsibility (CSR). Sustainable development and community-led initiatives in the hills of Uttarakhand have been at the centre of his work.

members.name: Pankaj Rawat
members.bio: A senior journalist and writer on the side of the people, Pankaj Rawat has spent 26 years telling the story of Uttarakhand's land, society and village life. Water, forests and land, the environment, migration, democracy and development have been at the heart of his journalism. His reporting brings the Himalayan village — its struggles, its concerns and its changes — vividly to life.

members.name: Chandrashekhar Kargeti
members.bio: Chandrashekhar Kargeti is a senior advocate, RTI activist and a watchful voice on matters of public interest. He has long worked on the right to information, transparency, good governance and citizens' rights. He is the legal advisor to Himalaya Samvad.

whoWeAre.title: Who we are
paragraphs: Himalaya Samvad is an independent Hindi monthly. Its purpose is to encourage serious, fact-based and constructive conversation on the social, cultural, environmental, educational, economic and development questions of the Himalayan region.
It is not a collection of news or events. It is an effort to bring forward the questions, worries, experiences and possibilities that shape the present and the future of the Himalaya and its people.

why.title: Why talk about the Himalaya?
paragraphs: The Himalaya is one of the most important mountain ranges on earth. It is not just a landform — it sustains the lives, culture, faith, water and livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people. Many of India's major rivers rise here, and a huge share of the country depends on the Himalaya, directly or indirectly.
Even so, Himalayan questions seldom get enough room in the national conversation. These are issues that need steady, serious and wide-ranging discussion.

quote.text: No society develops through plans, budgets and projects alone. It develops through aware citizens, thoughtful debate and people taking part together.

paragraphs: Himalaya Samvad was conceived with exactly these needs in mind. Lasting, meaningful change becomes possible only when a society talks openly about its problems, listens to different points of view and works its way towards answers. Himalaya Samvad is a modest attempt to strengthen that process.

commitment.title: A forum for dialogue — not for any party or ideology
commitment.subtitle: The Himalaya's problems are complex, and their solutions will have many sides. That is why there has to be room for dialogue, and for both agreement and disagreement.

localVoices.title: A platform for voices from the remote hills
paragraphs: The experiences, struggles, achievements and new ideas of remote mountain areas often never reach the mainstream. Teachers, health workers, farmers, women's groups, young entrepreneurs, social workers, researchers and local communities working in the villages have a great deal to teach the rest of us.
We want their stories to reach a wider audience, so that the conversation about development is not just about numbers but about people's lives.

publish.title: What you'll find in the magazine
publish.text: We give the research and analysis of experts the same weight as the experience of ordinary citizens and the realities on the ground — because knowledge doesn't live only in universities and institutions; it lives in society too.
publish.bridge: A bridge between research and society.

youth.title: For young people
youth.text: A new generation in the Himalayan regions is shaping its identity between education, jobs, technology, enterprise and global opportunity. We don't want young people to stay readers only — we want them to be writers, researchers, conversation-starters and part of the change.

global.title: Local, and beyond
global.text: The future of the Himalaya is not only a matter for the Himalayan states. Water, climate, biodiversity, natural resources and ecological balance matter to the whole country and to the world.

closing.text: Himalaya Samvad is more than a magazine. It is an ongoing effort — to connect ideas, to move the conversation forward and to look for what's possible. A better future starts with asking questions, and the answers come out of conversation.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: Himalaya Samvad respects the privacy of your personal information. This policy explains what we collect, why we collect it and how we use it.

sections.title: What we collect
paragraphs: We collect the details you give us when you sign up or fill in a membership, contact or advertising form — such as your name, email, mobile number, city and address.
Basic technical information from normal use of the site (such as your browser type) may be recorded for security and to improve the site.

sections.title: How we use it
paragraphs: We use your information to run your account, process memberships, reply to your messages and — if you agree — to tell you about new issues and events.
We do not sell your personal information to anyone.

sections.title: The online magazine and security
paragraphs: To protect the online edition, pages may carry a faint watermark linked to your account. Its only purpose is to discourage unauthorised sharing of the content.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: You can ask to see, correct or delete your information at any time by writing to info@himalayasamvad.in. You can leave the email bulletin whenever you like.

sections.title: Contact
paragraphs: For any questions about this policy, write to info@himalayasamvad.in.

terms.title: Terms of Use
terms.intro: By using the Himalaya Samvad website and online magazine, you agree to the following terms.

sections.title: Ownership of content
paragraphs: All articles, images and designs published on the website and in the magazine belong to Himalaya Samvad or the respective authors. They may not be republished or distributed without written permission.

sections.title: Using the online edition
paragraphs: The online magazine is for personal reading only. Downloading it, copying it, circulating screenshots or sharing it on any other platform is a breach of these terms.
Each account is for the use of one person only.

sections.title: Authors' views
paragraphs: Views expressed in published articles are the authors' own. The editorial board does not necessarily share them.

sections.title: Submitting work
paragraphs: Work sent to us must be original. The editorial board has the final say on what is selected for publication.

sections.title: Changes
paragraphs: These terms may change from time to time. Updated terms will always be published on this page.
